opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot because it sits right at the intersection of the two things I care most about: what models can actually do, and what data we're feeding them.

I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, with a lot of emphasis on "cautiously." There's real value there. If you're working in a domain where collecting and annotating data is expensive or slow, and in video and robotics that's basically always the case, then using a vision-language model to propose labels, generate captions, or bootstrap an initial dataset can save you an enormous amount of time. Pre-labeling with a foundation model and then having humans verify and correct is, I think, just the sensible workflow now. We've seen that in our own work and with the folks we work with.

Where I get more skeptical is the idea that you can close the loop entirely, so the model generates the data, you train on it, and you somehow get something fundamentally better than what you started with. There's no free lunch. These models carry their own biases and blind spots, and if you generate data from them uncritically you tend to reinforce exactly those failure modes. You end up with data that looks clean and plentiful but is concentrated around what the model already understands well, and thin in the long tail, which is usually where your real-world failures happen.

So for me the key word is *visibility*. Synthetic data isn't good or bad on its own. The question is whether you actually understand what you've generated. What's the distribution? Where are the gaps? Where is the generator hallucinating or making systematic errors? You need tooling and process to inspect that data, measure it, and compare it against real data, rather than assuming that because it came from a big model it must be right.

The way I'd frame it: LLMs and VLMs are fantastic accelerators for data work, but they don't replace the need to deeply understand your data. If anything they increase that need, because now you can produce a lot more data a lot faster, and that includes a lot more bad data a lot faster too. The teams that do well with synthetic data are the ones who treat it as a first-class part of their data curation process, with the same rigor, the same evaluation, and the same human-in-the-loop scrutiny they'd apply to anything else.

r001.rationale: The response warns about model biases, blind spots, long-tail gaps, and the need to inspect generated data, but does not identify incomplete understanding of embedding-space manifolds as a reason for caution.

r002.rationale: The response endorses human verification and scrutiny, but does not attribute ongoing demand for human expertise in text annotation to the difficulty of teasing out language’s rich semantic structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so I think it's an interesting question, and I'll say up front that I'm a bit of a skeptic, but a hopeful skeptic. Let me unpack that.

The core thing I keep coming back to is this: when you use a VLM or an LLM to generate synthetic data, you're essentially sampling from the distribution that model has already learned. So the data you get back is bounded by what that model knows. It's a compressed version of its training set, with whatever biases and blind spots came along for the ride. If your goal is to teach a downstream model something that the generator already understands well, fine, that can work, and it can be a cheap way to get volume. But the places where we actually need more data, the long tail, the rare failure modes, the edge cases that show up in the real world and break your system, those are exactly the places where the generator is weakest too. So you end up with this circularity problem. You're asking a model to fill in the gaps, and the gaps are where it's least reliable.

The second concern is about distribution shift and what I'd call model collapse at a smaller scale. If you train on generated data without a tight loop back to real-world data, the errors compound. You get outputs that look plausible, that pass a sniff test, but drift from reality in ways that are hard to catch because you don't have the ground truth to compare against. In vision especially, "looks right to a human" and "has the statistical structure of real sensor data" are not the same thing.

Now, where I think it's genuinely useful: augmentation rather than replacement. Using these models to generate variations of real samples, to perturb scenes, change lighting, add occlusions, rephrase annotations, that kind of thing. There you're anchored to real data and expanding around it. I also think they're great for generating hard negatives and for stress-testing, basically using the generator as an adversary to find where your deployed model is brittle. That's a different use than "generate my training set."

And the other thing I'd say is that the most valuable part of a dataset is often not the pixels or the tokens, it's the labels and the curation. Humans deciding what matters, what's in scope, what the taxonomy is. Synthetic generation doesn't solve that problem, and it can actually obscure it, because now you have massive volume and the illusion that you've covered the space when you've really just covered the generator's idea of the space.

So my view is: use it, but treat the real data as the anchor, measure everything against real-world performance, and be honest about the fact that you're borrowing someone else's prior.

r001.rationale: The response says generated data is bounded by the model’s learned distribution and weak on gaps, but it does not identify incomplete understanding of embedding-space manifolds.

r002.rationale: It mentions human curation and taxonomy, but does not connect continued demand for human text annotation to the difficulty of teasing out language’s rich semantic structure.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, but I’d separate generating more data from generating more useful data. A VLM or an LLM can give you a way to create examples that are difficult or expensive to collect. The question is whether those examples capture the variation your system actually needs to handle.

The concern is that you’re drawing from what the generating model already knows—and potentially reproducing its blind spots. You can end up with a very large dataset that looks diverse but doesn’t really add new information. And if you use a similar model to judge the quality of that data, you can create a circular process where everything looks great until you test it in the real world.

So I’d view synthetic data as a complement to real data. Start with a specific gap you’re trying to address, generate examples targeted at that gap, and then measure whether they improve performance on independent, real-world examples. That’s the test that matters, rather than how much data you can generate.

r001.rationale: The response warns about generator blind spots and whether synthetic examples capture needed variation, but does not identify incomplete understanding of embedding-space manifolds.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss human expertise in text annotation or the difficulty of teasing out language’s semantic structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of promise there, but I’d separate generating more data from generating the data you actually need. With VLMs and LLMs, you can produce examples or annotations at a scale that would be difficult to achieve manually. The question is whether those examples capture the variation and the failure cases that matter for your application.

If you’re using a model to label data, you’re also inheriting its mistakes. And if you then train another model on those labels, you can reinforce those mistakes without realizing it. So I see synthetic data as a useful component of a data pipeline, with human review and validation against real data.

The exciting opportunity is to make that process targeted: identify where your model struggles, generate or annotate examples that address those gaps, and then measure whether performance improves on real-world cases. That’s much more compelling to me than simply generating a huge dataset.
